title: Free Online Courses 免费网课
instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.
discussion_text:
Three academics are discussing free online courses and the reasons behind low enrollment numbers.
Speaker 1 (Academic - Promising) [Male]: Honestly, looking at the global data, it's amazing how many free online courses are available and really promising nowadays. They could be a total game-changer for higher education. But I honestly can hardly believe that so few people have enrolled this semester. The low participation and high drop rate across the board are just shocking to me.
Speaker 2 (Academic - Skeptic) [Female]: Well, I’m not entirely surprised. I think there's a major issue with initial trust here. When people see a platform offering a full syllabus for absolutely nothing, they immediately think it is too good to be true. They get deeply concerned about course quality, or worse, they suspect it is a scam or useless altogether.
Speaker 3 (Academic - Practical) [Male]: True, those doubts exist, but I think the bigger hurdle is practical rather than theoretical. It's not just about trust. Many students do not have time to commit to these programs because they are constantly juggling jobs and family obligations. They clearly have the desire to study, but the reality of a large amount of work in their daily lives stops them from finishing.
Speaker 1 (Academic - Promising) [Male]: That's a fair point, but don't get me wrong—online teaching requires a lot of design and deliver well. It requires a lot of effort from the faculty to set up. For individuals who cannot attend traditional school due to their difficult financial situation, these free platforms can be a lifeline! It’s such a very good idea, so it frustrates me that the completion rates are so abysmal.
Speaker 2 (Academic - Skeptic) [Female]: But that’s exactly the root of the problem. Because these modules are free, students face absolutely no financial punishment if they choose to quit halfway through. When a student pays thousands in tuition, they stay invested. Here, the only penalty is to yourself, which makes it way too easy to just walk away when things get busy. We really need to find other ways to build accountability in these virtual classrooms.
Speaker 3 (Academic - Practical) [Male]: Exactly, and we should also look at structural flexibility to accommodate their busy schedules. If universities could reschedule these courses to other times, like late evenings or weekends, we could easily attract more outsiders to join. Right now, a lack of promotion is also an issue; half the working professionals who need these skills don't even know these options exist.
Speaker 1 (Academic - Promising) [Male]: Mmm, I completely agree. Better scheduling and targeted marketing would definitely help pull in those outside demographics.
Speaker 3 (Academic - Practical) [Male]: Yeah! And we need to make sure the curriculum focuses on what they actually need. We want students to choose these modules because they are genuinely interested in it, and not because they are easy to pass. They need to see the real-world value, which is why we should design more practical over theoretical courses.
Speaker 2 (Academic - Skeptic) [Female]: Agreed. If we can fix the quality control, resolve the initial trust issues, and build a better framework for accountability, these free online courses might finally live up to their true potential.

Oh, by the way, Belle, can you remind me to pick up my laundry from the basement later? I keep forgetting.
Speaker 2 (On-Campus): Haha, yeah, I’ll text you later about the laundry. But about housing, I'm 100% coming back next year. In fact, I already put in my request for a single room on campus. I just think there’s a much better atmosphere for studying here. Plus, I absolutely hate commuting. The thought of waiting for the bus in the rain during a cold winter morning sounds completely miserable to me.
Speaker 3 (Off-Campus): Hmm, I see your point, but I'm strongly considering living outside the campus grounds this time. I definitely prefer a bit more independence than what the dorm rules allow. I actually found a pretty affordable place just a few blocks away, and it’s a great opportunity to experience more of the city rather than just staying inside the university bubble all day.
Speaker 1 (Indecisive): Ugh, you both make great points, which makes this even harder! I’m so nervous about submitting the response to the housing portal. They explicitly said room allocation is on a first-come basis, so I need to finalize my housing choice today if I want to beat the deadline.
Speaker 3 (Off-Campus): Well, why don't you sit down and make a list of pros and cons? That always helps me clear my head when I'm stuck. And hey, if you get completely desperate, you can always just flip a coin!
Speaker 1 (Indecisive): No way, I am not letting a coin decide where I live for a whole year!
Speaker 2 (On-Campus): Good call, don't do that. For me, looking at the stress of apartment hunting makes me even more set on staying in uni accommodation. Having 24/7 library access right down the hall is a lifesaver during exams. And honestly, not having to sign a lease or deal with standard landlords saves so much time. I can just focus on meeting up with my favorite study group.

instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.
discussion_text:
参考对话：
Two students and a student services officer are discussing applying for a student exchange programme at university.

I logged onto the application website last night and the whole process just looks a bit overwhelming. I’m honestly terrified that I’m going to confuse the steps and miss some important deadlines.
Will (Speaker 2 - Officer): Don't panic, Alice! It definitely seems like a lot to take in at first glance, but my job is to help you break it down into manageable steps. We provide clear checklists and info sessions throughout the month designed exactly to keep you on track so you don't miss a thing.
Charlotte (Speaker 3 - Student): Phew, that makes me feel a bit better. I actually started poking around the portal last week, too. Right now, I'm just trying to pick a place, but I'm completely torn between three different countries. It's so hard to find a destination that offers a good academic fit for my major while also being somewhere I genuinely want to experience.
Will (Speaker 2 - Officer): To help narrow it down, Charlotte, your very first step should be looking into the credit transfer process. Our university has specific agreements with certain partner universities overseas. Because of this, you must work closely with academic advisor teams to ensure your course selections approved before you even book a flight.
Alice (Speaker 1 - Student): Ah, right! That makes sense. I really want to go somewhere in Asia to get a completely different cultural experience, but I absolutely need to make sure those classes will count for my degree. I really can't afford to delay my graduation timeline.
Charlotte (Speaker 3 - Student): Exactly. But besides the credits, my absolute biggest worry is the financial side of moving abroad. When you look at the overall cost of living in some of these host cities, plus the actual cost of flights and tuition, it starts to look completely out of reach for a student budget.
Alice (Speaker 1 - Student): Oh, tell me about it! This isn’t just about saving up a small budget for a holiday; covering daily living expenses for a whole six months is a massive commitment. I’m already struggling financially with just my local expenses this semester, and I really don’t want to completely rely on my parents to bail me out.
Will (Speaker 2 - Officer): Those are incredibly valid concerns, but that’s precisely why early financial planning is key. The university offers a variety of specialized scholarships and bursaries specifically to help offset travel costs for exchange students. There are even some external grants available if you look in the right places, but you need to apply early to secure them.
Charlotte (Speaker 3 - Student): Wow, hearing that is seriously reassuring, Will. I had no idea the university offered that much support. I really want to do this programme for my own personal growth and independence, so knowing there are ways to manage the costs makes it feel worth the effort.
Alice (Speaker 1 - Student): Me too! I'm much more motivated to tackle that overwhelming portal now.
Will (Speaker 2 - Officer): Glad to hear it. Why don't you both come down to the global lounge for our official info session this Thursday? We can look at those checklists together and get your applications moving forward.
Charlotte (Speaker 3 - Student): Perfect. I’ll definitely see you there.
Alice (Speaker 1 - Student): Same here. Thanks a lot, Will!

title: Phone in Class 课上用手机
instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.
discussion_text:
参考对话：
Three teachers are discussing whether students are allowed to use smartphones in class.
Speaker 1 (Prohibit): I honestly think smartphones should be prohibited in our classrooms entirely. Every single day, my students are getting disturbed by texts vibrating on their desks, and this phenomenon really bothers me during lectures. It completely ruins the lesson flow. I want to stipulate that they must switch off their devices the moment they walk through the door.
Speaker 2 (Educational Use): Oh, come on, a total ban is a bit extreme. We can actually teach them to use them for educational purposes. For instance, some of my foreign students check words on translation apps because they are not good at English yet. It actually helps them better understand what we teach, and it allows the class to be lively and interactive.
Speaker 3 (Distraction/Policy): True, but you have to admit it’s incredibly easy to get distracted by social media instead of studying. There are serious negative effects of constant multitasking on a student's brain. If we aren't careful, their concentration and grades will completely suffer.
Speaker 1 (Prohibit): Exactly! It completely drives me crazy when they hide their screens under the desk and start chatting with others. As a teacher, you never know what they are doing down there! This screen addiction is everywhere now—just look at them playing on the phone during meals in the cafeteria. They don't know how to disconnect.
Speaker 3 (Distraction/Policy): Yeah, that’s a fair point. If we do allow them, it shouldn't turn into a free technology tutorial where we constantly waste lesson time trying to discourage them from scrolling. That's why consistency is key. If they can't use educational apps responsibly to do interactions, then devices should strictly be phones off and out of sight.
Speaker 2 (Educational Use): But wait, we have to consider our own habits too. Sometimes teachers are glued to their own devices during break duties, and that hypocrisy sends a mixed message to the kids. Instead of fighting it, we should evolve with technology. If they need to look up information for a group project, let them use it, and then simply tell them to put it away after that.
Speaker 1 (Prohibit): That sounds good in an ideal world, but it doesn't work in reality. We absolutely need a strict, school-wide policy so all students know they have to adhere to them across all subjects. I’m telling you, making them deposit their phones in a caddy at the entrance results in an immediate shift in focus and engagement. It forces everyone to realize we are part of the same learning community.
Speaker 2 (Educational Use): Hmm... I wouldn't mind a designated phone storage area by the door if it’s handled flexibly. Why don't we pilot this in a few classes next term first? That way, we can see if students still get distracted without completely cutting off beneficial digital resources.
Speaker 3 (Distraction/Policy): Oh, I like that idea! If we pilot it, we can gather some research from our own trials to see if there's any improved student performance. It’s definitely not necessary to put a ban if we can find a middle ground. Let's present this proposal at the next staff meeting to get everyone on board.

instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.
discussion_text:
参考对话：
Three students are discussing the pros and cons of online classes.
Speaker 1 (Anti-Online): I was looking at our timetable options for next semester, and I seriously can't stand online classes anymore. During my last remote module, my Wi-Fi would also cut out constantly, and the presentation slides freeze all the time. On top of that, I kept getting distracted by my phone, so I ended up missing half the content because I couldn't focus on the screen.
Speaker 2 (Pro-Online): That's a shame, but I actually prefer online learning over sitting in a crowded lecture theatre. For one thing, there's no more rushing out the door just to catch the 8am bus. I don't have to waste time commuting, and there is no spending money on cafeteria food either. I can just attend class in my pajamas and focus on taking notes in my comfortable room.
Speaker 3 (Hybrid/Campus): I get the convenience, but I chose this university for the campus experience, not to stare at little boxes on a screen all day. When everything is remote, it feels like we are all just lost in the digital void. I definitely learn better through face-to-face interactions because you can actually read body language and feed off the dynamic classroom energy.
Speaker 2 (Pro-Online): You have to consider the flexibility it offers, though. If you don't grasp a concept immediately, you can easily review lecture recordings later, even while eating dinner. It saves me nearly two hours every day on travel alone. Because of that comfort, I actually feel less intimidated and participate more online than I ever would in person.
Speaker 1 (Anti-Online): That might work for some, but I really value engaging in person. In a real classroom, if I have a question, I can just raise my hand and get immediate answers, whereas last week I typed a query in the chat and the professor didn't see it at all. Plus, real group discussions are so much better. Online breakout rooms are just awkward and unproductive, usually filled with dead silence and blank screens.
Speaker 3 (Hybrid/Campus): Exactly, those blank screens make it impossible to make friends or network properly. I actually failed a course last year when it was fully remote because I couldn't stay motivated alone. That’s why I strongly favor a hybrid over fully online approach. Having a schedule that is primarily in-person ensures we still get some campus experience while keeping things organized.
Speaker 2 (Pro-Online): A hybrid model could be a fair compromise, I suppose. It still allows those who live far away to study in their comfortable room for part of the week while avoiding the daily mad rush. As long as we can still access the recorded material to rewatch difficult parts, I think it balances the saving of time and money quite well.
Speaker 1 (Anti-Online): I could live with a hybrid system as long as the core seminars are face-to-face. I just need that external environment to keep me away from being distracted by my phone. Having real, spontaneous group discussions without technical glitches like frozen slides making us miss half the content is crucial for my learning.
Speaker 3 (Hybrid/Campus): Definitely. A hybrid model with a primarily in-person focus seems like the best path forward. It keeps us from getting lost in the digital void, lets us absorb that dynamic classroom energy, and ensures we don't miss out on the genuine university life we all signed up for. Let's make sure we select the blended streams when enrollment opens.

title: The Final Exam 期末考试
instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.
discussion_text:
参考对话：
Three students are debating the value of final exams versus continuous assessment.
Speaker 1 (Anti-Exam): I was just looking over our syllabus for next term, and it really got me thinking—final exams feel so outdated these days. Last semester was an absolute nightmare for me because I had three finals on the same day. I felt completely overwhelmed with memorizing facts, formulas, and dates just to pass. It felt more like a memory test than actual education.
Speaker 2 (Pro-Project): You're so right, and those traditional exams just encourage cramming the night before, which doesn't help us retain knowledge long-term. Instead of written tests, we should be assigned projects or research papers. Working on real-world projects forces us to think critically about the subject matter rather than just skimming through textbook chapters for a grade.
Speaker 3 (Pro-Exam): I see your points, but look at it this way—finals definitely serve a purpose in our academic development. Preparing for a massive exam forces us to review the entire semester's content from start to finish. It’s a highly valuable opportunity to consolidate everything we’ve learned into a big, cohesive picture before moving on to the next year.
Speaker 2 (Pro-Project): That sounds good in theory, but the extreme pressure actually causes many students to forget everything a week after the test is over. So many of my classmates suffer from severe anxiety because of this. Plus, traditional exams feel isolating and artificial, unlike real-world projects that allow for creativity and collaboration.
Speaker 1 (Anti-Exam): Exactly! Building on your point about isolation, the stress is often so intense that you can just panic and completely blank during the exam itself. I realized afterwards that I didn't truly understand most of what I wrote down. Judging a student's entire semester based solely on their performance under pressure like that is simply not real learning.
Speaker 3 (Pro-Exam): That might happen to some, but completing a major final exam also gives you a fantastic sense of closure at the end of the term. Walking out of that exam hall brings a massive sense of accomplishment. Furthermore, studying for them helps teach discipline and crucial time management skills that we'll always need in our careers.
Speaker 2 (Pro-Project): Well, I still believe that utilizing diverse evaluation methods would create a more equitable system for everyone, especially those who excel practically. After all, when we finally step into the real world, our employers will ask us to deliver successful projects, not sit quietly for standardized tests.
Speaker 1 (Anti-Exam): Absolutely, which is why a continuous assessment model would be much better because we could absorb material gradually week by week. Exams turn our education into a high-stakes game where one bad day completely ruins your GPA. We should focus on achieving a deep understanding of concepts instead of just regurgitating information on a test sheet.
Speaker 3 (Pro-Exam): To be fair, from an institutional view, exams are necessary because they are efficient for grading fairly. A standardized exam is an objective way to review the full scope of a student's knowledge while maintaining academic standards. However, I do agree that a mix of both methods would probably work best for a balanced curriculum.

title: Management of Assignment 作业规划
instruction: You will hear three people having a discussion. When you hear the beep,summarize the whole discussion. You will have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to give your response.
discussion_text:
参考对话：

 Three students are discussing strategies for managing their written assignments.



Speaker 1: Honestly guys, I’ve been feeling a lot of pressure lately because I find it hard to organize everything for our upcoming courses. Every single time I write a goal down, I just cannot stick to it for long. I never do it consistently, and I always end up losing momentum halfway through, which completely stalls my progress.

Speaker 2: I used to have that exact problem until I started using a breakdown method. Now, whenever we get lengthy assignments, I immediately break them into smaller ones. I make a plan, create an outline, and schedule everything step by step. Dealing with bite-sized tasks makes the workload feel much less intimidating.

Speaker 3: That's a solid strategy. For me, I prefer a routine-based method where I allocate different amounts of time depending on whether a task is urgent or difficult. I also try to work when I feel the most productive. Personally, I work best at night, especially in the evening after dinner when things quiet down.

Speaker 1: I wish I could do that, but I keep getting sidetracked by the smallest things, and then my whole plan falls apart. I think I'm really missing an external structure in my life. Without someone checking in on me, I just don't have that immediate accountability to keep my head down and focus.

Speaker 2: Distractions are definitely the enemy. If you get distracted, it will take longer to finish anything. That's why when I follow my schedule, I actively avoid mobile phones, TV, and checking emails. It requires a structured yet flexible approach, but making a conscious effort to try to focus without technology nearby helps immensely.

Speaker 3: Absolutely, and sticking to that routine is what helps you stay consistent and avoid last-minute stress. By setting mini-deadlines for each part of the work, you aren't rushing at the end. I’ve noticed that when I don't leave things to the final hour, it significantly improves the overall quality of my work.

Speaker 1: You both make excellent points. This is exactly why I think I need to have a work buddy. Having someone working right next to me would give me that vital sense of responsibility. If we push each other, I won't get sidetracked as easily, and it will force me to build better habits.

Speaker 2: That is a fantastic idea! Why don't we do the next assignment together? We can plan together and get motivated, and we can even practice as a group. Combining my step-by-step strategy with your need for a study partner sounds like a perfect win-win situation to keep us all on track.

Speaker 3: I’m completely on board with that. Having a study group is perfect because it keeps us accountable to one another. Plus, we can share ideas and feedback on each other's work before submitting it. It gives Speaker 1 the external structure they need while helping all of us maintain consistency. Let's do it!

I totally messed up the dates and accidentally wrote next Monday in my diary. Now it's too late to ask for help, and I’m facing extremely limited time to get all this research done.

I was facing a similar nightmare because I have a huge load of assignments due all at once this week, and to make things worse, I’m currently packing to move house. Speaker 1: You're so lucky to get that extra time. For me, it's way too late to ask my professor now, so I’ve just got to push through the night and finish it. The whole process of planning and organizing events before the term started was a massive commitment, but it allowed me to meet so many new people. Seeing everything come together has been really fulfilling.
Speaker 2: I completely agree, time is just slipping away! For me, volunteering at the campus library has been focused heavily on the organizational aspect. Like your role, it comes with its own unique challenges and rewards. I've gained truly valuable skills in cataloguing and event planning, and it gives me a genuine sense of giving something back to our community.
Speaker 3: That sounds wonderful. My experience working at the animal shelter has been quite different, mainly because it demands so much physical energy. It requires a lot of emotional resilience to stay focused on helping them heal.
Speaker 1: Exactly, but the upside is how much we grow. This experience has significantly developed my leadership and public speaking skills. It also relies heavily on teamwork to ensure every animal is well taken care of. Dealing with a variety of personalities has really improved how I'm managing my time.
